# **Fri Nov 13 (A4 due)** - Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)

ANCOVA is applied to data situations that require both ratio and nominal scale
explanatory variables. This topic is discussed in Dr. Schneider's notes [here](https://davidcschneider.github.io/StatisticalScience/LNotes/Pt4/Ch14_1.pdf). 

One important use is to compare two or more regression lines.

ANCOVA demonstrates the use of categorical along with ratio scale variables within
the framework of the general linear model. The categorical variable is species (_D.
persimilis_ or _D. pseudoobscura_).

The ratio scale variable is change in heterozygosity
with altitude. This example also shows the logic of interaction terms, which are
examined before main effects.

## Introduction
The next application of the general linear model compares two functions expressed as
straight lines. The data are from Dobzhansky (1948) as reported in Brussard (1984).
Theodosius Dobzhansky collected data on inversion heterozygosity (assuming Hardy
Weinberg equilibrium) of 3rd chromosome inversions from two species of fruit fly, from
Yosemite Park, California.

Inversion heterozygosity is a measure of genetic variability,
which is the raw material that natural selection acts on to produce descent with
modification (Darwinian evolution). Thus, the origin and maintenance of genetic
variability is one of the central questions in population biology.

What factors generate or
erode genetic variability? Harsher environments at higher altitudes are expected to select
for narrower range of phenotypes, hence reduce genetic variability. Does genetic
variability decrease at higher altitude, due to stronger selection in extreme environments?
Does the heterozygosity gradient differ in two co-occuring species of fruitfly _Drosophila
persimila_ and _Drosophila pseudoobscura_?

## Model

**Verbal model** Inversion heterozygosity decreases with altitude, depending on species.

## Data

```{r}
species.alt.data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/heteroz-alt-species.csv")
species.alt.data
```

```{r,warning=FALSE}
require(ggplot2)
g1=ggplot(species.alt.data, aes(x = elevation_km, y = heterozygosity, color = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3)+xlab("elevation (km)")+theme_classic()
g1
```


```{r}
species.alt.model <- lm(heterozygosity ~ species + elevation_km + species*elevation_km, data = species.alt.data)
summary(species.alt.model)
anova(species.alt.model)
```

```{r}
g2=g1+geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, fullrange = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal() + ggtitle("ANCOVA: Effect of elevation on heterozygosity for two fly species")
g2
```

```{r}
coef(species.alt.model)
beta0 = unname(coef(species.alt.model))[1]
beta.sp = unname(coef(species.alt.model))[2]
beta.elev = unname(coef(species.alt.model))[3]
beta.int = unname(coef(species.alt.model))[4]

elevation = species.alt.data$elevation_km

beta1.line = beta0 + elevation*beta.elev
beta2.line = (beta0 + beta.sp) + elevation*(beta.int + beta.elev)
beta3.line = (beta0+beta0+beta.sp)/2 + elevation*(beta.elev +beta.int + beta.elev)/2
species.alt.data = data.frame(species.alt.data, beta1.line, beta2.line)

g2 +geom_line(data=species.alt.data, aes(y=beta1.line), color = "black", linetype="dashed")+geom_line(data=species.alt.data, aes(y=beta2.line),color = "grey", linetype="dashed")+geom_line(data=species.alt.data, aes(y=beta3.line),color = "violet", linetype="dashed")

```
